title: Malaysia’s climate-finance programme turns on who absorbs early project risk
summary: Bank Negara Malaysia Deputy Governor Adnan Zaylani argued that Islamic finance could fund a greater share of climate investment if institutions could redistribute the risks that deter private capital at the outset. The financing problem was not simply a shortage of green bond issuance. Developing an unproven technology, financing a small supplier’s emissions measurement and insuring a farmer against a flood involve different risks and cash-flow profiles. The deputy governor offered Malaysian examples of risk sharing, technical assistance and takaful, the Islamic form of protection, to illustrate how those constraints might be addressed. He spoke at the launch of a World Bank and Islamic Development Bank report and attributed its cross-country findings to that report (opening remarks and three findings).

The financing requirement was particularly large for poorer members of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. According to figures Zaylani drew from the report, investment needed for low-carbon strategies averaged 1.4% of GDP and exceeded 5% in low-income OIC economies. He judged that public resources alone could not meet that scale. One difficulty was access to early-stage capital. Only 3% of the companies that obtained private-equity or venture funding for clean and climate technologies during 2017–2024 came from the OIC, accounting for just 0.5% of global investment in the comparison. The first figure counts firms; the second describes funding. Neither measures the realised return on OIC climate projects. An additional impediment lay in insurance: some takaful providers lacked the actuarial expertise and data infrastructure for parametric cover against events such as floods and droughts (opening discussion of the report).

Malaysia illustrated the distinction between capital-market issuance and financing by participating institutions. The country introduced the first green sukuk in 2017; Zaylani put subsequent green and sustainability sukuk issuance at more than 47 instruments worth USD 13.4 billion. Separately, 18 members of the Value-Based Intermediation community had channelled more than USD 11 billion into Islamic green financing. The speech did not reconcile the instrument and financing totals or establish that the underlying exposures were disjoint. They show that intermediaries can mobilise capital, but cannot establish on their own which investments were incremental, who retained the risk or how the financed assets performed (discussion of Malaysia and its 13th Plan).

The i-CITA initiative, introduced the preceding September, goes further into the structure of financing. A RM100 million government fund supplies matching finance to participating Islamic banks piloting risk-sharing contracts. Zaylani argued that reducing the initial risk to banks could help them participate in climate and food-security projects whose cash flow was poorly matched to fixed instalments or substantial collateral requirements. The stated fund size is public support capacity; the address gives no drawdown, loss-sharing waterfall or private capital multiple. The Climate Finance Innovation Lab administered by Bank Pembangunan Malaysia was similarly designed to test new financing structures and demonstrate feasibility before wider use. A working pilot and a portfolio of independently financeable projects represent different stages of that process (discussion of i-CITA and the innovation lab).

Smaller enterprises account for 97% of Malaysian business establishments. Many face the climate requirements of large supply-chain customers with limited capacity to document their own emissions. The Greening Value Chain Programme, Low Carbon Transition Facility and Greening Halal Businesses Programme combined financial access with practical support, including carbon accounting and technical guidance. Of the participants reported for the value-chain programme, 2,890 SMEs had attended training and more than 250 had measured and reported greenhouse-gas emissions. Those figures establish participation and reporting. They do not establish an emissions reduction or a gain in the firms’ profitability (discussion of SMEs).

The paddy crop takaful scheme illustrates a distinct use for risk transfer. By March 2025, RM16.2 million, reported as USD 4 million, in compensation had been approved for 6,319 affected farmers. This is a dated cumulative measure of approved compensation, separate from the later government commitment to i-CITA. It shows a mechanism through which disaster losses can be shared, while leaving key questions about premiums, payout speed, coverage gaps and long-run viability open. Zaylani situated these initiatives in a broader case for public interest and climate resilience in Islamic finance. For an investor, the evidence supports examining each instrument’s allocation of risk; it supplies no relative-value conclusion on sukuk or evidence that an individual issuer’s borrowing cost has fallen (closing discussion of takaful and public interest).

questions.question: Which risks does the matching fund transfer, and would the projects obtain private finance without it?
questions.detail: The address identifies RM100 million in government matching finance and a reduction in early risk for participating banks. It leaves the ranking of claims, ultimate loss allocation and private mobilisation unspecified. These terms matter to a lender’s expected cash flows. Seek i-CITA eligibility rules, contract terms and programme-level disbursement data, then distinguish genuinely additional lending from existing commitments brought under the pilot.

questions.question: Do the green sukuk and bank-financing totals correspond to additional productive assets?
questions.detail: The speech reports substantial issuance and financing through a practitioner group without reconciling the two populations. An investor assessing scale or impact needs issuer-level use of proceeds, refinancing shares, project completion and operating cash flows. Begin with sukuk prospectuses and allocation or impact reports, checking for overlap with the banks’ green-financing disclosures and separating commitments from actual disbursements.

questions.question: How effectively does takaful stabilise farm cash flow following a disaster?
questions.detail: Approved compensation shows that protection can be activated. It provides little evidence about payment timing relative to expenses, premiums relative to farm income or losses falling outside cover. These determine whether farmers can continue servicing debt after a shock. Compare scheme terms, aggregated claims timelines and weather or loss data with the March 2025 approvals cited in the address.
